lesson.title: Same Address, Nearest Answer: How Anycast Routing Works
lesson.summary: Anycast routing lets several physically separate servers share one IP address and relies on ordinary shortest path routing to send each client to whichever instance the network considers closest.
lesson.body:
Anycast assigns the same IP address to multiple servers in different physical locations, and unlike multicast, which delivers a packet to every member of a group, anycast delivers each packet to exactly one instance, whichever one the network judges to be closest to the sender. The two ideas sound similar because they both start from one address representing many machines, but they solve opposite problems: multicast is about reaching everyone in a group, anycast is about reaching just one, the nearest one.

What makes anycast work is that it needs no new routing machinery at all. It simply reuses the ordinary shortest path routing algorithm that every router already runs. Each anycast server, or a router near it, announces the same address prefix into the routing system, for example through BGP. Every router elsewhere just treats those announcements the way it treats any other set of competing routes to the same destination and runs its normal best path selection process. Whichever announcement comes out on top of that process, by AS path length, by IGP cost, by whatever metric the routing algorithm already uses, is the one that wins, and it can be a different announcement for routers in different parts of the network. The result is that clients in different regions transparently end up talking to different physical servers, all without any central load balancer making that decision.

This is also what makes anycast cheap to operate and self healing. If one instance goes down, it simply stops announcing the address, the announcement is withdrawn, and routers around the network reconverge to the next nearest instance using the exact same shortest path process they always use, no special failover logic required.

It is worth being precise about what "nearest" means here: it is nearest by the routing protocol's metric, not necessarily nearest by geography or by actual measured latency. Two paths with the same number of BGP hops can have very different real world delay, so anycast can occasionally send a client to an instance that is technically closer by the metric but not the fastest in practice. This is also why anycast pairs best with short, stateless exchanges: if the underlying routing were to shift mid conversation, a long lived connection could in principle be redirected to a different physical server that has no idea the conversation was ever happening.

The clearest real world example is the DNS root server system. The address 198.41.0.4, known as a.root-servers.net, is announced from many sites around the world at once. A resolver in Tokyo and a resolver in Frankfurt both send their query to the exact same address, 198.41.0.4, but land on two different physical machines, because each router along each path independently ran its own routing algorithm and picked its own closest announcement.
